title: A wife at the well (Genesis 24:1–27)
hook: the servant's test: the one who offers water to him and to his camels too

segments.voice: Last week ended with Sarah's burial, and a grave bought at full price, because grief deserves ground.

Abraham is old now, and Isaac needs a wife. Abraham sends his senior servant, the elder of his house, back to the family's homeland, with ten camels loaded with gifts. The servant arrives outside a town at evening, the hour when the young women come out to draw water, and makes the camels kneel by the well. And he's stuck. How do you pick a person for someone else's whole life? He prays, in the old JPS translation: "O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, send me, I pray Thee, good speed this day, and show kindness unto my master Abraham." Abraham has told him where to look: among the family. But which young woman? He sets a test. Not looks. Not money. Something much smaller, and much harder to fake.
screen: `TEN CAMELS AND A LONG ROAD.` → `EVENING AT THE WELL.` → `HOW DO YOU CHOOSE?`

segments.voice: I'll ask a girl for a drink, he says. If she answers, drink, and I'll water your camels too, she's the one. Before he's even finished praying, Rebekah comes out with a jar on her shoulder and fills it. He runs up and asks for a sip. She says, drink, my lord, and hurries to lower the jar. Then, without being asked: "I will draw for thy camels also, until they have done drinking." Ten camels, every one of them thirsty. That's trip after trip down to the spring, jar after jar, for a stranger's animals. The Torah says she ran. That's chesed. It's a big word in the Hebrew Bible, and hard to translate: kindness, loving-kindness, loyal love, mercy. At its heart, chesed is kindness that goes past what's owed: past fair, past asked. The servant's prayer uses it: show chesed to my master. And when he realizes she's the one, he bows and blesses God, who has not forsaken His mercy, chesed again. The prophet Micah later sums up what God asks of a person: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly. That mercy is chesed. The Mishnah says the whole world stands on three things: Torah, worship, and acts of loving-kindness. The servant wasn't looking for someone who'd do what was asked. He was looking for someone who'd notice the camels.
screen: `DRINK, AND YOUR CAMELS TOO.` · `TEN THIRSTY CAMELS.` · `CHESED — KINDNESS PAST WHAT'S OWED.` · `THE WORLD STANDS ON THREE THINGS.` · then, large: `I WILL DRAW FOR THY CAMELS ALSO.`

segments.voice: Think of the requests people make of you in a day: pass the salt, send me that file, can you pick up milk. Then look for the camels behind one of them, the thing nobody asked for that would make their day lighter: the coworker who asked for the file but is clearly drowning, the parent who asked about dinner but is lonely. Picture the extra thing; if you pray, you can ask to notice.
Chesed. Loving-kindness: kindness that goes past what's owed. Rebekah watering ten camels for a stranger.
Your line: water the camels too. Ten camels, one jar, and she ran. Fifty days now.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness such as visiting the sick, comforting mourners and helping a bride and groom, among the pillars of Jewish life, and communities often organize them through volunteer groups.

what a scholar hears: chesed in the servant's prayer (24:12, 24:14, 24:27), in Micah 6:8's love mercy, and in Pirkei Avot 1:2's acts of loving-kindness.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 24:12 and 24:19.
The servant is unnamed in chapter 24; tradition identifies him as Eliezer (15:2). The script calls him 'his oldest servant' (24:2). Confirm.
'A thirsty camel can drink an astonishing amount' kept vague on purpose (figures of 25–40 gallons are commonly cited).
Micah 6:8 paraphrased ('to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly'), not marked as a JPS quotation; confirm and consider quoting if exact.
Pirkei Avot 1:2 (Simon the Righteous): Torah, avodah, gemilut chasadim. Confirm.
